tspan.tspan: Simulating Antarctic sea ice with a surprisingly
simple statistical model
Elio Campitelli
(1) School of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment, Monash University, Australia.
(2) Securing Antarctica’s Environmental Future, Monash University, Australia.
elio.campitelli@monash.edu
Did 2024 Antarctic sea ice concentration anomalies
contribute to the stratospheric warming event?

text.tspan: Extremely simple model of sea ice growth and melt
Integrating the model

tspan.tspan: Figure 1
: Mean monthly change in sea-ice concentration at each gridpoint as a function of
monthly sea-ice concentration and monthly 2-metre temperature in hexagons. The black
contours represent the statistical model, whose coefficients are shown in the table to the right.
Observations of Antarctic sea-ice concentration (NSIDC CDR) and 2-metre temperature
(ERA5) show some of the qualitative characteristics expected from the simple model as
schematised on the left plot (theoretical model in dashed lines).
For T
a
> T
f
, melt is low both at high C due to the insulating effect, and at low C because
there is little ice left to melt. In mid C, there is enough ice-free ocean to allow heat
exchange and enough ice to melt, so melt is fast.
For T
a
< T
f
, growth is slow at high C both due to the insulating effect and because there
is
little open ocean to freeze, but at low C it's fast because there is no insulation and a lot
of
water to freeze over.
A particularity not explained by the model is that the effective freezing point depends on
the sea-ice concentration (purple line).
The ocean surface exchanges heat with the atmosphere but sea-ice insulates the
process.
So the heat flux is proportional to the temperature difference and the ice-free
area (1-C).
When there is ice, ocean temperature is close to the freezing point, so we
assume
constant temperature. If the flux is positive (ocean gains heat), then the ice melt
and the
change in sea-ice concentration is proportional to the flux and sea-ice
concentrations
themselves. If the flux is negative (ocean loses heat), then the ice-free
area freezes, so the
change is proportional to the flux and the ice-free area.
Figure 1
: Zonal mean zonal wind anomalies between 65°S and 55°S (shading) and zonal
mean temperature anomalies (contours) south of 60°S in winter 2025. In mid July and in

text.tspan: early August mean temperature increased suddenly by more than 15K. Zonal wind also
decreased by up to 35m/s. In August, the wind anomalies reached the surface.
Figure 1: Zonal mean zonal wind
anomalies between 65°S and 55°S
(shading) and zonal mean temperature
anomalies (contours) south of 60°S in
winter 2025. In mid July and in early
August mean temperature increased
suddenly by more than 15K. Zonal wind

August, the wind anomalies reached the

The tropical ocean was the main driver of the persistent anticyclonic anomalies over the

tspan.tspan: Amundsen sea in April-May 2024. Sea ice played a minor role, if any.
Antarctic sea ice responds extremely quickly to the oceanic and atmospheric forcing.
Previous research using atmosphere-only models fail to account for this important effect.

text.tspan: Research on the effects of Antarctic sea ice on atmospheric circulation should use fully
couple models to account for this fast response.
Conclusions

tspan.tspan: The statistical model is a prognostic model of sea-ice concentration at each gridpoint
based on current sea-ice concentration and 2-m temperature. I integrate the model using
initial conditions from January 1981 and using ERA5 2-m temperature as forcing on a
25km resolution grid.
Figure 2:
Monthly sea-ice extent anomalies observed (red) and simulated by this simple

text.tspan: model (green). Hindcast from the current S2S model at the Bureau (ACCESS-S2) is shown
for comparison in blue.

tspan.tspan: This simple model achieves comparable correlations with
observations as the coupled model.
It's bias in the Summer is strikingly similar to ACCESS-
S2. This could suggest that the coupled model is
missing the same processes that I'm ignoring.
An important limitation of this model is that it
severely underestimates the local variability of
sea-ice concentration.
